title: Conditions with if, [[ ]] and case
summary: Branch on a command's exit status with if, test strings, numbers, and files with [[ ]] and (( )), and match patterns with case.
intro: So far your scripts ran every line, with `&&` and `||` for small choices. `if` runs a block of commands only when a condition holds, and `case` picks one branch by matching a value against patterns. A condition is just a command: `if` looks at its exit status, so `grep -q`, `[[ ]]`, and `(( ))` all work as tests. The folder your script runs in holds a small project, with `config.ini`, `deploy.sh`, `hosts.txt`, and the folders `logs/` and `build/`.

steps.title: if, commands and [[ ]]
steps.body:
`if` runs a command and looks at its exit status. 0 runs the `then` block. Anything else tries each `elif` in order, then the `else` block. `fi` closes it:

```bash
if grep -q db-1 hosts.txt; then
  echo "db-1 is in hosts.txt"
else
  echo "no db-1"
fi
```

`[[ ]]` is the command made for tests. On strings: `==` and `!=`, `-z` for empty, and `-n` for not empty, and a glob on the right of `==` matches like a file name. On files: `-e` exists, `-f` is a file, `-d` is a folder, `-s` exists and isn't empty, `-r`, `-w`, and `-x` can be read, written, and run, `-L` is a symlink, and `a -nt b` is newer. `&&`, `||`, and `!` combine tests inside it:

```bash
file="logs/app.log"
if [[ -f $file && $file == *.log ]]; then echo "a log file"; fi
if [[ ! -e notes.txt ]]; then echo "no notes.txt"; fi
```

You'll also see `[ ]` and `test`, the older forms. They split an unquoted variable into words, so an empty one leaves a gap and the test breaks. Inside `[[ ]]`, variables never split.

examples.title: A command as the condition
examples.prompt: Check the app log for errors with `grep -q`, then pick the worst kind of line it has with `elif`.
examples.code:
if grep -q ERROR logs/app.log; then
  echo "errors found: $(grep -c ERROR logs/app.log)"
else
  echo "clean"
fi

if grep -q FATAL logs/app.log; then
  echo "fatal errors found"
elif grep -q WARN logs/app.log; then
  echo "no fatal errors, but warnings"
else
  echo "clean"
fi
examples.output:
errors found: 3
no fatal errors, but warnings
examples.explanation: `grep -q` prints nothing. It exits 0 when it finds a match and 1 when it doesn't, and `if` only looks at that status. The log has ERROR lines, so the first `if` runs its `then` block. It has no FATAL line, so the second `if` moves on to the `elif`, whose `grep` finds WARN lines. The `else` block would run only if every test before it failed.

examples.title: File tests
examples.prompt: Check three things about the project, print a line for each, and exit 1 if any check failed.
examples.code:
status=0

if [[ -d build ]]; then
  echo "ok: build is a folder"
else
  echo "fail: build"
  status=1
fi

if [[ -L current ]]; then
  echo "ok: current is a symlink"
else
  echo "fail: current"
  status=1
fi

if [[ -s empty.txt ]]; then
  echo "ok: empty.txt has content"
else
  echo "fail: empty.txt is empty"
  status=1
fi

exit "$status"
examples.output:
ok: build is a folder
ok: current is a symlink
fail: empty.txt is empty
examples.explanation:
`build` is a folder and `current` is a symlink to it, so the first two checks pass. `empty.txt` exists, but `-s` also needs at least one byte, so the third check fails and sets `status` to 1. Each check prints its line and moves on, so you see every problem at once, and `exit "$status"` ends the script with 1 because something failed. Times work too: `a -nt b` is true when `a` changed more recently than `b`. Every file here starts with the same time, so this snippet first gives two files times of their own with `touch -d`, which sets a file's time and creates the file when it doesn't exist:

```bash
touch -d '2026-10-18 09:00' last-deploy.stamp
touch -d '2026-10-19 08:30' build/VERSION
if [[ build/VERSION -nt last-deploy.stamp ]]; then echo "the build changed after the last deploy"; fi
```

examples.title: Strings, and why [[ ]]
examples.prompt: Compare strings with `[[ ]]`, then try a test with `[ ]` on an empty variable.
examples.code:
env="prod"
name=""
file="logs/app.log"

if [[ $env == prod ]]; then echo "env is prod"; fi
if [[ $env != dev ]]; then echo "env is not dev"; fi
if [[ -z $name ]]; then echo "name is empty"; fi
if [[ $file == *.log ]]; then echo "$file ends in .log"; fi
if [[ $file == "*.log" ]]; then echo "quoted: match"; else echo "quoted: no match"; fi

[ $name == guest ]
examples.output:
env is prod
env is not dev
name is empty
logs/app.log ends in .log
quoted: no match
examples.explanation: `*.log` on the right of `==` is a glob, so it matches any name that ends in `.log`. Quoted, `"*.log"` is plain text and only matches a name that really is `*.log`. The last line uses the old `[ ]`. `name` is empty and unquoted, so it disappears, and `[` sees only `== guest`. It reports `unary operator expected` and exits 2, which ends this script with 2. `[[ $name == guest ]]` would just be false.

practice.title: Preflight
practice.prompt:
Check that the project is ready to deploy. Print one line per check, `ok: NAME` when it passes or `fail: NAME` when it doesn't.

1. `config.ini` exists and isn't empty.
2. `logs` is a folder.
3. `deploy.sh` is executable.
4. Exit with status 1 if any check failed, or 0 when all of them passed.

Check also runs your script on a copy of the project with problems, and from an empty folder.

Expected output:

```text
ok: config.ini
ok: logs
ok: deploy.sh
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: check that config.ini exists and isn't empty, and print ok: or fail:

# TODO: check that logs is a folder

# TODO: check that deploy.sh is executable

# TODO: exit 1 if any check failed
practice.solution:
status=0

if [[ -s config.ini ]]; then
  echo "ok: config.ini"
else
  echo "fail: config.ini"
  status=1
fi

if [[ -d logs ]]; then
  echo "ok: logs"
else
  echo "fail: logs"
  status=1
fi

if [[ -x deploy.sh ]]; then
  echo "ok: deploy.sh"
else
  echo "fail: deploy.sh"
  status=1
fi

exit "$status"

tests.output:
ok: config.ini
ok: logs
ok: deploy.sh

fail: config.ini
ok: logs
fail: deploy.sh

fail: config.ini
fail: logs
fail: deploy.sh

hints: Use one `if`/`else` per check, as in the file tests example: `-s` for a file that exists and isn't empty, `-d` for a folder, and `-x` for executable.
Start with `status=0`, set `status=1` in every `else`, and end with `exit "$status"`.

steps.title: Numbers and regex
steps.body:
For numbers, use `(( ))`. It compares with `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, and `!=`, and names inside need no `$`:

```bash
count=12
if (( count > 10 )); then echo "more than 10"; fi
```

`[[ ]]` has its own number tests, `-eq`, `-ne`, `-lt`, `-le`, `-gt`, and `-ge`, which you'll see in many scripts. Never use `<` or `>` inside `[[ ]]` for numbers: there they compare text, character by character.

`=~` matches a regular expression. Put the regex in a variable and leave it unquoted on the right, since a quoted regex is matched as plain text. What each group in parentheses matched lands in `BASH_REMATCH`: `${BASH_REMATCH[0]}` is the whole match, `${BASH_REMATCH[1]}` the first group, and so on:

```bash
re='^([a-z]+)-([0-9]+)$'
host="web-12"
if [[ $host =~ $re ]]; then
  echo "role ${BASH_REMATCH[1]}, number ${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
fi
```

Each match replaces `BASH_REMATCH`, so copy the groups into variables before you match again.

examples.title: Numbers, not text
examples.prompt: Compare 12 with 10 two ways, then see what `[[ 9 > 10 ]]` says.
examples.code:
count=12
if (( count > 10 )); then
  echo "(( )): $count is more than 10"
fi
if [[ $count -gt 10 ]]; then
  echo "-gt: $count is more than 10"
fi

if [[ 9 > 10 ]]; then
  echo "[[ 9 > 10 ]] is true: it compares text"
fi
if (( 9 > 10 )); then
  echo "(( 9 > 10 )) is true"
else
  echo "(( 9 > 10 )) is false: it compares numbers"
fi
examples.output:
(( )): 12 is more than 10
-gt: 12 is more than 10
[[ 9 > 10 ]] is true: it compares text
(( 9 > 10 )) is false: it compares numbers
examples.explanation: `(( count > 10 ))` and `[[ $count -gt 10 ]]` both compare numbers, so both agree that 12 is more. `[[ 9 > 10 ]]` is a bug on purpose: inside `[[ ]]`, `>` compares text the way `sort` orders it, character by character, and `9` comes after the `1` of `10`. So it says yes. ShellCheck, the Bash linter, warns about that line, which is why this example turns it off. `(( ))` reads both sides as numbers and gets it right.

examples.title: Capture groups
examples.prompt: Split a version tag into its three numbers, work out the next minor version, then try a tag that doesn't fit.
examples.code:
re='^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$'

tag="v2.14.0"
if [[ $tag =~ $re ]]; then
  major=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
  minor=${BASH_REMATCH[2]}
  patch=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}
  echo "major $major, minor $minor, patch $patch"
  echo "next minor: v$major.$(( minor + 1 )).0"
fi

tag="release-2.14"
if [[ $tag =~ $re ]]; then
  echo "match: $tag"
else
  echo "no match: $tag"
fi
examples.output:
major 2, minor 14, patch 0
next minor: v2.15.0
no match: release-2.14
examples.explanation: `^` and `$` make the regex cover the whole tag, `\.` is a literal dot, and each `([0-9]+)` is a group of digits. After a match, `BASH_REMATCH` holds what the groups matched, and copying them into `major`, `minor`, and `patch` keeps them safe from the next match. `$(( minor + 1 ))` turns 14 into 15. `release-2.14` doesn't start with `v` and has only two numbers, so `=~` fails and the `else` runs.

examples.title: Validate input
examples.prompt: Read two ports, one per line, and stop with status 2 at the first one that isn't a whole number from 1 to 65535.
examples.code:
read -r port
read -r admin_port

if [[ $port =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && (( port >= 1 && port <= 65535 )); then
  echo "port: $port"
else
  echo "invalid port: $port"
  exit 2
fi

if [[ $admin_port =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && (( admin_port >= 1 && admin_port <= 65535 )); then
  echo "admin port: $admin_port"
else
  echo "invalid admin port: $admin_port"
  exit 2
fi
examples.explanation: A short regex can be written as is, unquoted: `^[0-9]+$` means only digits, from start to end. `&&` runs `(( ))` only when the regex matched, which matters: to `(( ))`, `80a` isn't a number but a broken expression, and it would print an error. `8080` passes both tests. `80a` fails the regex, so the `else` prints its message, and `exit 2` stops the script with status 2, a common code for bad input.

practice.title: Version bump
practice.prompt:
Read two versions, the old one and then the new one, and say which part went up.

1. Read the two lines. A valid version looks like `v1.4.2`: a `v`, then three whole numbers with a dot between each.
2. If either one isn't valid, print `invalid` and exit with status 2.
3. Otherwise print `major` if the new major number is bigger. Print `minor` if the majors are equal and the new minor is bigger, and `patch` if the majors and the minors are equal and the new patch is bigger. Print `none` in every other case.

Input:

```text
v1.4.2
v1.5.3
```

Expected output:

```text
minor
```
practice.starter:
re='^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$'

# TODO: read the old version, then the new one

# TODO: if the old one doesn't match re, print invalid and exit 2
# TODO: otherwise copy its three numbers out of BASH_REMATCH

# TODO: do the same for the new one

# TODO: print major, minor, patch, or none
practice.solution:
re='^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$'

read -r old
read -r new

if [[ ! $old =~ $re ]]; then
  echo "invalid"
  exit 2
fi
old_major=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
old_minor=${BASH_REMATCH[2]}
old_patch=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}

if [[ ! $new =~ $re ]]; then
  echo "invalid"
  exit 2
fi
new_major=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
new_minor=${BASH_REMATCH[2]}
new_patch=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}

if (( new_major > old_major )); then
  echo "major"
elif (( new_major == old_major && new_minor > old_minor )); then
  echo "minor"
elif (( new_major == old_major && new_minor == old_minor && new_patch > old_patch )); then
  echo "patch"
else
  echo "none"
fi
hints: Match each version with `[[ $old =~ $re ]]`, and copy `${BASH_REMATCH[1]}` to `${BASH_REMATCH[3]}` into variables right away, as in the capture groups example: the next match replaces them.
Compare with `(( ))`, never `>` inside `[[ ]]`. As text, `10` comes before `9`.
Use one `if`/`elif`/`else` chain, and make each branch require the bigger parts to be equal: `elif (( new_major == old_major && new_minor > old_minor ))`.

steps.title: Match patterns with case
steps.body:
`case` compares one value against patterns, top to bottom, and runs the commands of the first one that matches. Each branch ends with `;;`, and `esac` closes the whole thing:

```bash
day="Sat"
case "$day" in
  Sat|Sun)
    echo "weekend"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "weekday"
    ;;
esac
```

The patterns are globs, the same as for file names: `*` matches anything, `?` one character, and `[Yy]` either letter. `|` separates alternatives. `*)` matches everything, so it goes last as the default. Since the first match wins, put specific patterns before general ones. A short branch fits on one line, like `stop) echo "stopping" ;;`.

`case` reads better than a chain of `elif`s whenever you're checking one value against several fixed choices: a command name, a file extension, a yes or no answer.

examples.title: Commands
examples.prompt: Pick what to do from the `ACTION` variable, which this example sets to `run`.
examples.code:
case "$ACTION" in
  start|run)
    echo "starting the worker"
    ;;
  stop)
    echo "stopping the worker"
    ;;
  status)
    echo "the worker is running"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: ACTION=start|run|stop|status" >&2
    exit 64
    ;;
esac
echo "done: $ACTION"
examples.explanation: `ACTION` comes from the environment, like the variables in the Parameter Expansion lesson. `start|run)` matches either word, so `run` starts the worker, and after `;;` the script carries on after `esac`. Any value no branch names falls to `*)`, which writes a usage message to stderr and exits with status 64, a code many tools use for wrong usage.

examples.title: File types
examples.prompt: Print how to look inside the file named in `FILE` without unpacking it.
examples.code:
case "$FILE" in
  *.tar.gz|*.tgz)
    echo "tar -tzf $FILE"
    ;;
  *.zip)
    echo "unzip -l $FILE"
    ;;
  *.gz)
    echo "zcat $FILE"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "cat $FILE"
    ;;
esac
examples.explanation: `logs-2026-10.tar.gz` matches `*.tar.gz`, so `case` prints the `tar` command and stops. It would match `*.gz` too, which is why the order matters: with `*.gz)` first, every tarball would get `zcat`. `*.tar.gz|*.tgz)` puts both spellings of a gzipped tarball in one branch, and `*)` catches every other file.

examples.title: Yes or no
examples.prompt: Ask whether to deploy, and accept any capitalization of yes.
examples.code:
read -rp "Deploy now? [y/N] " answer

case "$answer" in
  [Yy]|[Yy][Ee][Ss])
    echo "deploying"
    ;;
  [Nn]*)
    echo "cancelled"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "no answer, so no deploy"
    ;;
esac
examples.explanation: Each `[Yy]` matches one letter in either case, so the first branch takes `y`, `Y`, `yes`, `Yes`, `YES`, and every other mix. `[Nn]*` takes any answer that starts with an n, like `no` or `nope`. Anything else, an empty line included, falls to `*)`, which is what the capital `N` in `[y/N]` promises: no is the default.

practice.title: Extract command
practice.prompt:
Print the command that unpacks the file named in the `FILE` environment variable. Run sends the first test's value, `FILE=site-backup.tar.gz`.

1. For a name ending in `.tar.gz` or `.tgz`, print `tar -xzf FILE`.
2. For `.tar.xz`, print `tar -xJf FILE`.
3. For `.zip`, print `unzip FILE`.
4. For any other `.gz`, print `gunzip FILE`.
5. For anything else, print `unknown: FILE` to stderr and exit with status 1.

In each line, FILE stands for the file's name.

Expected output:

```text
tar -xzf site-backup.tar.gz
```
practice.starter:
# FILE comes from the environment, like FILE=site-backup.tar.gz
# TODO: print the command that unpacks FILE, with one case

# TODO: for anything else, print unknown: FILE to stderr and exit 1
practice.solution:
case "$FILE" in
  *.tar.gz|*.tgz)
    echo "tar -xzf $FILE"
    ;;
  *.tar.xz)
    echo "tar -xJf $FILE"
    ;;
  *.zip)
    echo "unzip $FILE"
    ;;
  *.gz)
    echo "gunzip $FILE"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown: $FILE" >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
esac
hints: Start from the file types example: one `case "$FILE" in` with a branch for each kind of name.
`case` takes the first pattern that matches, and `*.gz` also matches `site-backup.tar.gz`. Put `*.tar.gz|*.tgz)` above `*.gz)`.
The last branch is `*)`, with `echo "unknown: $FILE" >&2` and then `exit 1`.

recap:
- `if CMD; then ...; elif CMD; then ...; else ...; fi` branches on an exit status, so any command can be a condition: `grep -q`, `[[ ]]`, or `(( ))`.
- `[[ ]]` tests strings (`==`, `!=`, `-z`, `-n`, globs like `*.log`) and files (`-e`, `-f`, `-d`, `-s`, `-r`, `-w`, `-x`, `-L`, `-nt`), and combines tests with `&&`, `||`, and `!`.
- Prefer `[[ ]]` to `[ ]` and `test`, which break on an empty, unquoted variable.
- Compare numbers with `(( a > b ))` or `-gt` and its friends, never with `>` inside `[[ ]]`, which compares text.
- `=~` matches a regex, kept in a variable and unquoted, and puts its groups in `BASH_REMATCH`.
- `case` matches one value against glob patterns, and the first match wins: `a|b)` for alternatives, `[Yy]*)` for either case, `*)` last as the default, and `;;` after each branch.
